title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
In this analysis, I look at Occupied housing unit numbers across counties in Florida, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.
vars <- load_variables(2023, "acs5")
View(vars)
Then use the search box.

my_state <- params$state      # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B25002_002"     # the variable code, in quotes B25002_002 Occupied Housing Units

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                     myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                     <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 12001 Alachua County, Florida  112776   1105  281751    NA
2 12003 Baker County, Florida      9012    295   28186    NA
3 12005 Bay County, Florida       76118   1106  181368    NA
4 12007 Bradford County, Florida   9104    367   27888    NA
5 12009 Brevard County, Florida  251889   1622  620533    NA
6 12011 Broward County, Florida  749372   2712 1946127    NA


Notice the column names: myvarE, myvarM, popE, popM. The E and M suffixes are estimate and margin of error.

county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         62        352728.
2 Moderate                 5         11947.


[What is the average population of high-confidence counties versus low-confidence counties? Is there a pattern?]
The average population of high-confidence counties is 352,728. The average population for low-confidence counties is 11,947. As a result, we can see that counties with fewer population will likely to end up in higher margin of error.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Address all three:

Which communities in your state do we know the least about? The ACS data suggest that we know the least about smaller communities in Florida, particularly Lafayette County and Liberty County. Lafayette County has the largest relative margin of error in my analysis, with a MOE of 8.82%, followed by Liberty County at 6.93%. In comparison, 43 of Florida’s 67 counties fall into my high-confidence category, while 19 are moderate and only 5 are classified as low confidence.
Why? This pattern is related to how the ACS is collected. Unlike a complete census, the ACS estimates population and housing characteristics from a sample of households. Smaller counties generally have fewer households and therefore fewer sampled households. With a smaller sample size, estimates are subject to greater sampling uncertainty, which can produce a larger margin of error relative to the estimate. My results illustrate this relationship: high-confidence counties have an average population of 352,728, while low-confidence counties have an average population of only 11,947.
What could go wrong? This uncertainty matters for public policy because agencies may treat all county-level estimates as equally precise. If funding were allocated based on occupied housing unit estimates without considering their uncertainty, smaller counties could be disadvantaged. Their estimates are less reliable, so policymakers might underestimate or overestimate their actual housing needs and allocate resources based on numbers that appear more certain than they really are.



Propagate the margin of error. If you compute a derived value — a percentage, a ratio, a sum — its uncertainty depends on the uncertainty of its inputs, and you can’t just carry the original MOE along. The Census Bureau publishes formulas for this, and tidycensus implements them: moe_sum(), moe_prop(), moe_ratio(). Compute something derived, and get its margin of error right.
Parameterize the report. Add params: to the YAML so the state is an input rather than hard-coded, and the same file regenerates for any state. Render it from the terminal with quarto render assignment2.qmd -P state:NY.
Write a function and iterate. Wrap the data pull in a function, then use purrr::map_dfr() to run it across several states at once. Does the small-places-are-noisier pattern hold everywhere, or are some states different?
Change the geographic scale. Run the same variable at geography = "tract" inside one county. Compare the margins of error to what you saw at county level. What does that imply about the resolution at which you can actually trust ACS data?

If you try one, add a short section describing what you did and what you found.

Done in the heading.

3, the small-places-are-noisier pattern holds for FL, NY, TX, OH, PA.

get_county_data <- function(state_abbr) {
  
  get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = c(
      occupied = "B25002_002",
      population = "B01003_001"
    ),
    state = state_abbr,
    year = 2023,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide"
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      state = state_abbr,
      estimate = occupiedE,
      moe = occupiedM,
      population = populationE,
      moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100,
      reliability = case_when(
        moe_pct < 2.5 ~ "High confidence",
        moe_pct < 5 ~ "Moderate",
        TRUE ~ "Low confidence"
      )
    ) %>%
    select(
      GEOID, NAME, state,
      estimate, moe, population,
      moe_pct, reliability
    )
}


states <- c("FL", "NY", "TX", "OH", "PA")

all_states <- purrr::map_dfr(
  states,
  get_county_data
)


state_result <- all_states %>%
  group_by(state, reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    avg_moe_pct = mean(moe_pct),
    median_moe_pct = median(moe_pct),
    max_moe_pct = max(moe_pct),
    occupied_housing = mean(estimate),
    pop = mean(population)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_moe_pct))

what i learned today (title)
Today, I learned about the logic behind how QMD and HTML work for humans and machines, respectively. QMD is easier for humans to read and write because it allows us to combine text, code, and formatting in one document. HTML, on the other hand, is the language that browsers use to understand and display the content.
I also learned the differences between Git, GitHub, and GitHub Desktop. Git is a version control system that helps track changes in a project. GitHub is an online platform where repositories can be stored and shared, while GitHub Desktop provides a more visual and user-friendly way to work with Git and GitHub.
Another important thing I learned today is the importance of maintaining a clean and organized folder structure. As projects become more complicated, it can be difficult to find files or understand which files are being used. Keeping folders organized from the beginning can make it easier to manage a project, avoid confusion, and collaborate with others.
Overall, today’s lesson helped me better understand how different tools and systems work together behind the scenes to support a digital project.
